evidence.quote: Were you approached by community and/or political party representatives?

claims.text: An ordinal binary record where an approach by community and/or political party representatives is either denied or affirmed, with no detail on who approached or what was said.

evidence.quote: Did you feel threatened during the interview?

claims.text: An interviewer-side binary registering the interviewer's own felt threat at the interview, an exposure state narrower than any physical act.

evidence.quote: Were you physically threatened during the interview?

claims.text: A binary on bodily threat specifically, separately asked from the felt-threat item, so the two can diverge in a single interview.

evidence.quote: Was he or she: honest, in between, or misleading?

claims.text: A three-point interviewer judgment of respondent honesty, running honest to in between to misleading, a perception of candor rather than an answer-accuracy test.

evidence.quote: should not be bound by laws or court decisions

claims.text: A forced-choice plus strength statement pair pitting presidential exemption from laws and court decisions against presidential obedience, recording a normative rule-of-law stance.

evidence.quote: should never intervene in the country's political process

claims.text: A forced-choice plus strength pair contrasting military non-intervention with legitimate takeover when elected leaders abuse power, a norm about the armed forces rather than an event report.
A single actor nomination from a fixed list assigning who should ensure elected MPs do their jobs, with President, Parliament or council, party, voters, no one, and non-substantive codes.
The president counterpart of the MP accountability item using the same actor list, so the two offices can be compared on one nominally shared scale.
A four-point likelihood that a woman candidate would face community criticism, name-calling, or harassment, an anticipated sanction rather than a recorded event.

evidence.quote: to advance the rights and equality of women

claims.text: A five-point effort judgment moving from much less to much more with about-right-amount in the middle, asking whether government action for women's rights is adequate rather than whether equality exists.

evidence.quote: most important for our government and society to address?

claims.text: A single-choice selection of the most important women's-rights issue, with education, workplace, representation, property, violence, other, and an explicit none-of-these option.

evidence.quote: temporarily limit democracy or democratic freedoms

claims.text: A five-point agreement that police and security enforcement of public health mandates is a justified temporary limit on freedoms, conditioned on a public-health emergency and carrying a prior-COVID non-applicability code.

evidence.quote: Who do you think sent us to do this interview?

claims.text: A respondent attribution of the interview's sponsor across a fixed list spanning the survey organization, research and private companies, NGOs, schools, media, party, government, international bodies, God, other, and no one.

evidence.quote: Willing to participate in follow-up surveys

claims.text: A consent-style willingness for follow-up contact whose not-applicable code separates respondents lacking a mobile number from those who declined.

inquiries.alternatives: An approach-affirming group whose threat reports run higher than no-approach interviews, together with any physical-threat report lacking a felt-threat report, would read threats as partly external pressure; a flat pattern would instead keep felt threat inside interviewer experience and disjoin the physical item from approach.
inquiries.ceiling: Asked-eligible interviewer-reported Yes/No items only; denominator is interviews where these items were administered, not all contacts; no statement about who approached, no causal effect, and no link to respondent answers.
inquiries.question: Do interviews reporting an approach by community or party representatives show higher felt-threat and physical-threat rates than interviews with no reported approach, and does physical threat ever occur without felt threat?

holds.missing: No country-level record of court-obedience controversies or military intervention history accompanies the rule-of-law and armed-forces norm items.
holds.why: Whether the presidential-obedience and takeover contrasts were live national controversies at fieldwork cannot be established from the item metadata.

holds.missing: No record of which health mandates, enforcement episodes, or gender-rights debates were contemporaneous with fieldwork.
holds.why: Whether respondents judged experienced conditions rather than hypothetical framings is not determinable from the question texts.

holds.missing: No recontact design or mobile-ownership documentation beyond the not-applicable code and sponsor list.
holds.why: Follow-up consent cannot be scaled to a recontact population, and perceived sponsorship cannot be checked against actual commissioning.

holds.missing: No interviewer debrief or incident log tying threat reports to later conduct or data quality.
holds.why: Any causal reading of threat reports against honesty ratings remains unsupported by separate item stems alone.
